examples: It's frustrating because we can't communicate.
The bus isn't coming, so it's frustrating.
The room is small, so it feels stuffy.
nuance: 답답하다 covers both a physical stuffy, closed-in feeling (a small room, tight clothes, a stuffy nose) and an emotional one — being frustrated when things don't go your way or you can't express yourself. As a 하다 adjective it conjugates to 답답해요. Newcomers often feel 답답해요 when 말이 안 통해서 (the language doesn't get through).
mistakes: Conjugating as 답답하요; 하다 adjectives become 해요, giving 답답해요.
Using it only for anger — 답답하다 is the stifled, frustrated feeling, while 화나다 is being angry.

examples: I ate a lot, so I'm full.
If you're full, please stop eating.
nuance: 배부르다 means your stomach is full after eating, the opposite of 배고프다 (to be hungry). It is a 르-irregular adjective, so the 르 becomes ㄹㄹ in the 요-form: 배불러요. Koreans often say it to politely show they enjoyed the meal and cannot eat more.
mistakes: Saying 배부러요; the 르-irregular doubles the ㄹ, giving 배불러요.
Confusing it with 배고프다 (hungry) — 배부르다 is the full, satisfied feeling.

examples: It's no fun when I'm alone.
nuance: 재미없다 is the opposite of 재미있다 (to be fun/interesting) and is written as one word. Use it for movies, games, classes, or any activity that bores you. The 없다 part already means 'there isn't', so never add 안 in front of it.
mistakes: Writing it as two words 재미 없다; the standard headword is one word, 재미없다.
Saying 안 재미없어요 to negate it — to say it IS fun, use the separate word 재미있어요.

examples: It tastes bad because it got cold.
If it tastes bad, you can leave it.
nuance: 맛없다 is the opposite of 맛있다 (to be delicious) and is written as one word. It is pronounced like [마덥따], with the ㅅ linking to the next syllable. Because 없다 already carries the negative meaning, you never put 안 before it.
mistakes: Pronouncing it letter-by-letter; the natural sound is [마덥써요] for 맛없어요.
Adding 안 (안 맛없어요) — to say it IS tasty, switch to 맛있어요.

examples: I feel at ease now that I'm home.
nuance: 편하다 describes both physical comfort (a comfy chair, comfy clothes) and ease of mind or convenience. It is the opposite of 불편하다. The adverb form 편하게 (comfortably) is very common in invitations like 편하게 드세요 (help yourself).
mistakes: Conjugating as 편하요; 하다 verbs become 해요, so it is 편해요.
Using it only for physical objects — it also means convenient (편한 교통, convenient transport).

usage: I feel unwell / my body is uncomfortable
also a polite way to say unwell
examples: If you're uncomfortable, please tell me.
nuance: 불편하다 is the opposite of 편하다 and covers physical discomfort (tight shoes), inconvenience (bad transport), and social awkwardness or feeling unwell. As a 하다 adjective it conjugates to 불편해요. It is a polite, common word for complaints.
mistakes: Saying 안 편하다 — while understandable, the natural single word is 불편하다.
Conjugating as 불편하요; 하다 adjectives take 해요, giving 불편해요.

examples: I'm upset because I did badly on the test.
I feel hurt hearing those words.
nuance: 속상하다 is the warm, everyday word for feeling upset, disappointed, or heart-sore — literally your insides (속) being hurt. It is gentler and more emotional than 화나다 (angry); you use it when something saddens or frustrates you. Koreans say it about small daily letdowns as well as bigger hurts.
mistakes: Confusing it with 화나다 (to be angry); 속상하다 is sad/disappointed, not furious.
Conjugating as 속상하요; as a 하다 adjective it becomes 속상해요.

usage: use 이/가 for the body part
examples: It's itchy, so I keep scratching.
nuance: 간지럽다 covers both the tickly feeling when someone tickles you and a light itchy sensation on the skin or in the throat. It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective, so 간지럽 + 어요 becomes 간지러워요. For a stronger itch you scratch, 가렵다 is often used instead.
mistakes: Conjugating as 간지럽어요; the ㅂ changes to 워, giving 간지러워요.
Mixing up the body-part particle — use 이/가 (등이 간지러워요), not 을/를.

examples: It's awkward because we just met.
Things are awkward between the two of them.
The new clothes feel awkward on me.
also used for things that feel unnatural
nuance: 어색하다 describes an awkward, uneasy feeling between people who are not yet close, or something that looks or feels unnatural. It is the opposite of 자연스럽다 (natural). As a 하다 adjective it conjugates to 어색해요 and is very common when meeting new people.
mistakes: Confusing it with 부끄럽다 (shy/embarrassed); 어색하다 is more about awkwardness and unfamiliarity.
Conjugating as 어색하요; 하다 adjectives become 해요, giving 어색해요.

usage: Nice to meet you / glad to see you
I'm really glad to see you
examples: It's good to hear your voice.
It's been a while, so I'm really glad.
오랜만이다 = it's been a long time
nuance: 반갑다 is the warm, happy feeling of meeting or seeing someone, and it powers the everyday greeting 만나서 반가워요 (nice to meet you). It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective, so 반갑 + 아요 becomes 반가워요. Use it for people, not for objects or events.
mistakes: Conjugating as 반갑아요; the ㅂ-irregular gives 반가워요.
Using it for general happiness — for that use 기쁘다; 반갑다 is specifically about meeting/seeing someone.

usage: use 이/가 for the body part
examples: It's itchy from a mosquito bite.
If it's itchy, put on some cream.
nuance: 가렵다 is the everyday word for an itch you want to scratch, on the skin, scalp, or anywhere on the body. It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective, so 가렵 + 어요 becomes 가려워요. It is stronger and more 'scratch-worthy' than the lighter 간지럽다.
mistakes: Conjugating as 가렵어요; the ㅂ becomes 워, giving 가려워요.
Marking the body part with 을/를 — use 이/가 (등이 가려워요).

english: to be a bother; annoying to do
usage: It's a hassle / I can't be bothered
examples: I can't be bothered to clean.
It's a hassle to go out.
Today everything feels like a bother.
nuance: 귀찮다 is the very common feeling of something being too much of a hassle or not worth the effort, like when you can't be bothered to get up or cook. It often pairs with a -기 noun form: 요리하기 귀찮아요 (cooking is a hassle). It is pronounced [귀차나요].
mistakes: Pronouncing the ㅎ; 귀찮아요 sounds like [귀차나요].
Confusing it with 피곤하다 (tired) — 귀찮다 is about not wanting the effort, not physical tiredness.

usage: Are you having a hard time?
nuance: 힘들다 covers anything physically or emotionally hard, tiring, or tough — a long day, a difficult job, or a rough time in life. With -기 it describes a hard task: 공부하기 힘들어요 (studying is hard). The ㄹ drops before endings starting with ㄴ/ㅅ, as in 힘드세요? and 힘드네요.
mistakes: Keeping the ㄹ in honorific form — it is 힘드세요?, not 힘들세요?.
Confusing it with 어렵다 (difficult to understand/solve); 힘들다 leans toward tiring or emotionally hard.

examples: I feel lonely when I'm alone.
I've been a bit lonely lately.
I'm lonely because I miss my family.
nuance: 외롭다 is the feeling of loneliness when you are alone or far from people you love. It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective, so 외롭 + 어요 becomes 외로워요. It describes an inner emotional state, unlike 심심하다 which is more about being bored with nothing to do.
mistakes: Conjugating as 외롭어요; the ㅂ-irregular gives 외로워요.
Confusing it with 심심하다 (bored); 외롭다 is emotional loneliness, not lack of activity.
